definition: The accuracy, completeness, consistency, and trustworthiness of data throughout its lifecycle.
The degree to which data conforms to the actual entity being measured or described.
The degree to which data contains all desired components or measures.
The degree to which data is repeatable from different points of entry or collection.
The process of storing data in multiple locations. Replicating data at different times or places risks the copies falling out of sync with each other.
The process of copying data from a storage device to memory, or from one computer to another. An interrupted transfer can leave an incomplete dataset.
The process of changing data to make it more organized and easier to read. Meant to make analysis more efficient, but an error during the process can compromise that efficiency.
A criterion that determines whether a piece of data is clean and valid.
A data constraint requiring values to fall between predefined maximum and minimum values.
A data constraint meaning a value can't be left blank or empty.
A data constraint meaning a value can't have a duplicate.
A data constraint requiring values to match a prescribed pattern, such as a phone number matching ###-###-####.
A data constraint requiring that certain conditions across multiple fields be satisfied, such as percentage values across fields adding up to 100%.
A database-only data constraint requiring a column's values to come from a defined set of discrete values, such as a status column only accepting Yes, No, or Not Applicable.

Data used as a substitute for the data you actually need, when that data isn't available or there isn't enough of it — for example, using sales data for a similar existing product to estimate demand for a brand-new one.
A way of selecting a sample from a population so that every possible type of the sample has an equal chance of being chosen.
The probability that a sample size accurately reflects the greater population. A 95% confidence level means that running the same survey 100 times would produce similar results 95 of those times.
The range of possible values the population's result would fall within at a study's confidence level — the sample result plus or minus the margin of error.
The percentage of people expected to complete a survey out of everyone who received it.
A process to determine if a survey or experiment has meaningful results.
The probability of getting meaningful results from a test, usually shown as a value out of one. A statistical power of at least 0.8 is typically considered the minimum for statistical significance.
A determination of whether a result could be due to random chance or not — the greater the significance, the less due to chance.
The maximum amount that a sample's results are expected to differ from those of the actual population.
Data that is incomplete, incorrect, or irrelevant to the problem being solved.
Data that is complete, correct, and relevant to the problem being solved.
Any data record that shows up more than once, often caused by manual data entry, batch data imports, or data migration.
Data that has been superseded by newer and more accurate information.
Data that is missing important fields.
Data that is complete but inaccurate.
Data that uses different formats to represent the same thing.
An indication that a value does not exist in a dataset — not the same as a zero, which is itself a value.
A spreadsheet tool that changes how cells appear when values meet specific conditions, such as highlighting blank cells.
A spreadsheet tool that automatically searches for and eliminates duplicate entries from a spreadsheet.
A tool for checking the accuracy and quality of data before adding or importing it.
A tool for determining how many characters can be keyed into a spreadsheet field.
A function that returns the length of a text string by counting the number of characters it contains — LEN in most spreadsheets, LENGTH in most SQL dialects, doing the same thing either way.
A function that returns a set number of characters from the left side of a text string.
A function that returns a set number of characters from the right side of a text string.
A function that returns a segment from the middle of a text string.
A spreadsheet function that joins together two or more text strings.
A function that removes leading and trailing spaces from a value; the spreadsheet version also collapses repeated spaces in between, while SQL's only strips the ends.
A spreadsheet function that divides text around a specified character and puts each fragment into a new, separate cell.
The process of combining two or more datasets into a single dataset.
How well two or more datasets are able to work together.
An agreement that unites two organizations into a single new one.
The process of matching fields from one data source to another.
The process of automating parts of a workflow, such as a script that flags missing values, to save time and increase productivity.
A keyword added to a SQL SELECT statement to retrieve only non-duplicate entries.
A SQL clause that sorts query results by a specified column, ascending by default or descending with DESC.
A SQL clause that caps the number of rows a query returns.
A SQL statement that adds new data into a database table.
A SQL statement that changes existing data in a database table.

A SQL statement that creates a new table in a database if one by that name doesn't already exist. Running a query doesn't itself save a table — the result has to be downloaded or saved into a new table separately.
A SQL statement that deletes a table from a database if it exists — good practice for cleaning up tables you created yourself so unused tables don't clutter the database.
A SQL function that extracts a portion of a text string, starting at a specified position for a specified number of characters.
A SQL function that converts data from one data type to another.
Converting data from one data type to another.
A SQL function that adds strings together to create new text strings that can be used as unique keys, such as combining a product code and a color.
A SQL function that returns non-null values from a list of columns, such as showing a product's name when it exists and falling back to its product code when the name is null.
A number that contains a decimal.
A process to confirm that a data-cleaning effort was well executed and the resulting data is accurate and reliable.
sequence: Go back to the original, unclean dataset and compare it against the cleaned data to spot common problems.
Manually clean up anything that remains, using tools like conditional formatting, filters, or Find and replace.
Step back and confirm the business problem, the project's goal, and that the data can actually solve it.

definition: A SQL statement that steps through one or more conditions and returns a value as soon as a condition is met — useful for correcting a misspelling in a new column without altering the underlying table.
A tool that finds a specified search term in a spreadsheet and replaces it with something else.
A spreadsheet function that counts the total number of values within a specified range, including non-numeric values (unlike COUNT, which counts only numerical values).

A checklist of common problems to run through during data-cleaning verification: sources of errors, null data, misspelled words, mistyped numbers, extra spaces and characters, duplicates, mismatched data types, inconsistent strings, inconsistent date formats, truncated data, and business logic.
The process of tracking the changes, additions, deletions, and errors involved in a data-cleaning effort.

A file containing a chronologically ordered list of modifications made to a project, typically recording what changed, a description, the date, who made and approved the change, a version number, and the reason for the change.
A system holding the official versions of shared queries or files, so a change can be synced to, reviewed, committed, and reverted if it causes a problem.
sequence: Sync to the most up-to-date version before making a change.
Have someone else review the change (a code review).
Submit the change to the repository (a code commit), documenting what changed and why.
Everyone else syncs to the newly updated version.
Revert to a previous version if the change causes a problem.

definition: Having someone else look over a proposed change to a shared query or file before it's committed, whether done formally or as simply as asking a senior analyst to take a look.
Submitting an updated version of a query or file to a shared repository in a version control system, typically documented with a comment describing what changed and why.
